items: Guggenheim Investments Private Debt Fund IV (‘PDF IV’ or ‘The Fund’) held its final close on March 31, 2026. The Fund closed on $4.5 billion in commitments, achieving its hard cap and notably surpassing the initial fundraise target of $3.0 billion.

2025 direct lending deal volumes represented the second-busiest year on record for private credit, with $81.4bn in buyout financing and record CLO formation at $43.1bn1. While deal count declined in 4Q25 year-over-year, dollar-based volumes rose, with Debtwire reporting an approximately 24% increase compared to the prior-year period2. Mega-deals (>$1bn deal size) were the primary driver - large LBO financings and BSL-to-private-credit migrations (i.e., Service Logic at $3.1bn and Pike Corporation at $3.0bn) lifted average deal size notably. In 4Q25, US direct lending activity captured $56.6bn in nominal terms across 189 deals, versus $66.3bn of activity across 206 deals executed in 3Q251.

There has been significant attention and media coverage paid to private credit BDCs and liquidity dynamics of semi-liquid vehicles. Guggenheim only manages private debt mandates for institutional investors, we do not manage any vehicles that are subject to redemption requests or forced liquidity provisions, insulating us from the selling pressures that are currently impacting managers of semi-liquid structures. We see opportunities emerging as peers facing redemption-driven liquidity needs are becoming forced sellers of high-quality assets at discounted prices. We remain optimistic that this dislocation may translate into attractive deal flow at compelling entry points over the coming quarters.

There has been healthy skepticism around software exposure in loan portfolios and the longer-term impacts of AI on the direct lending market. The recent attention around software risks exposes concerns that we have held for some time. We were deploying more capital into software deals in the ~2016-2020 timeframe and we have been underweight compared to broader market volumes in more recent years as we have found less relative value amid a more crowded backdrop. Software credits in PDF IV continue to perform well with portfolio companies delivering approximately 20% average EBITDA growth since deal time with an average loan-to-value of 31%, providing a significant equity cushion to our loans3. We recently held a webcast to discuss what we are seeing in the market around this topic wherein we shared our AI risk framework that we run every credit through before we make an investment. If you were unable to attend the software/AI webcast or would like to receive the recording, please let us know.
Consistent with our process over the last 20+ years, we remain focused on finding compelling relative value in fundamentally sound companies.

Our diverse origination capabilities spanning sponsor relationships and non-sponsored opportunities allow us to see a wide cross-section of deal flow beyond the mega-sized transactions that dominated headlines in Q4. We continue to employ a patient approach prioritizing credit quality and seeking out superior risk-adjusted returns from both a pricing and documentation perspective.

PDF IV deployed $1.6 billion across 18 credits in 2025. This capital was deployed at an average spread of S+544. Guggenheim was the lead investor on 91% of capital deployed in 2025, the sole lender on 33% of invested capital, and 92% of the capital invested in these deals has a financial maintenance covenant3. We feel that these stats underscore our disciplined approach to origination, structuring, and sourcing downside protections.

Despite spread compression at the top of the market, we continue to find pockets of compelling risk-adjusted returns, particularly in the core middle market where competitive dynamics remain more favorable. Median spreads on acquisition-related deals held steady in the S+450-475 range in 4Q25, and we continue to source deals well above these levels on average with stronger structural protections. PIK as a percentage of net investment income in PDF IV is currently 3.0%, versus 24.0% among the 13 largest BDCs through 4Q254.
Please see the enclosed case studies for additional information on the deals closed in 4Q25.

blocks.html: Investment Risks. The Assets discussed herein are not suitable for all investors. An investment in any Asset is speculative and involves a high degree of risk. The Assets discussed herein may engage in leveraging, short sales and other speculative investment practices that may increase the risk of investment loss. Investments in middle market loans, bank loans and other floating rate securities involve special types of risks, including credit risk, interest rate risk, liquidity risk and prepayment risk. An Asset’s exposure to high yield securities may subject investors to greater volatility. Some asset-backed securities, including mortgage-backed securities, may have structures that make their reaction to interest rates and other factors difficult to predict, making their prices very volatile and they are subject to liquidity risk. Assets may invest in derivative instruments, which may be more volatile and less liquid, increasing the risk of loss when compared to traditional securities. A potential conflict of interest may arise when GCF or any of its affiliates participate in loan arrangements for which it is providing investment management services, investment banking services or other transaction related services and in which the strategy also invests.
